title: It Just Got a Lot Cheaper to Try Gemini Spark, Google's AI Agent
body:
Pranay Parab
                            
        
            Pranay Parab
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePranay Parab is an independent tech journalist based in Mumbai, India. He covers tech for Lifehacker, and specializes in tutorials and in-depth features.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Google
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Gemini Spark, the AI agent built into Google Gemini, is now a lot cheaper to try out in the U.S. Previously, Gemini Spark was exclusive to the Google AI Ultra plan, which costs $100-$200 per month. The company is now bringing the agentic AI to its AI Pro plan, which costs $20 per month. (For now, this change is exclusive to the U.S.)When Gemini Spark was announced during Google I/O 2026, its features seemed potentially useful, but the barrier to entry was too high for most people. That appears to be changing now, as Google has cut the price by as much as 90%. It is not yet available on the $5/month AI Plus plan or the free tier, but that could change in the future too—though it's likely that using Gemini Spark on lower pricing tiers could mean that you hit your usage limits much faster.What is Gemini Spark?Google Gemini is a chatbot and a voice assistant that answers your questions, creates text, media, and even entire apps for you. Gemini Spark takes those capabilities to your Google account and executes actions for you.
You can think of Gemini Spark as a personal AI assistant that can look at your emails, calendar entries, photos, and other data in your Google account to perform tasks on your behalf. You can use Spark to bulk unsubscribe from mailing lists, make flight bookings, send reminder emails to clients, colleagues, or family members, book appointments, and much more. Having said all that, a Gemini Spark overview from out sister site PC Mag emphasizes that its features tend to overlap with Gemini. PC Mag called Spark the best AI agent yet, but that doesn't mean it's perfect.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Does Gemini Spark respect your privacy?To someone who is even remotely privacy-conscious, using Gemini Spark is going to sound quite invasive: You basically have to give it access to your entire computer if you want it to be able to act on your behalf. Google is aware of that, and has programmed the AI agent to ask for confirmations before performing certain actions. If you ask the agent to find birthday photos from 2017 and email them to someone, for example, Gemini Spark will show you the pictures and ask for a confirmation before actually sending the email. It applies the same logic to deleting emails, sending messages, using your saved credit cards to pay for reservations, and more.It's worth keeping in mind that AI services have created serious problems for people who use these apps without due caution. The biggest strength of Gemini is its access to all the data that’s in your Google account, but if you give it unrestricted access and the AI agent messes up a request, you could be stuck with an incorrect hotel reservation, a flight booked to a wrong country, or other serious consequences.

After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel.         Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Cheng Xin/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple just released the second public betas of both iOS 27 and macOS 27,
                                            While the macOS 27 update seems to be mostly small improvements to performance and stability, the latest iOS 27 release did introduce some more substantive changes.
                                            Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, and Liquid Glass are the marquee features coming with the "27" software versions.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple just released the second public betas of both iOS 27 and macOS 27—only a week after the launch of public beta 1—so anyone signed up for the beta program can now test the latest public version of the software on their compatible iPhones and Macs. The biggest features coming to iOS 27 and macOS 27 are related to Siri AI, Apple Intelligence tools, and Liquid Glass customizations, as well as performance upgrades; so if you don't want to wait until the full release in the fall to try these out, you can install the public betas as they become available. iOS 27 and macOS 27 public beta 2 updatesLast week, Apple released iOS 27 and macOS beta 4 for developers, which 9to5Mac notes are the same build as public beta 2. While the macOS 27 update seems to be mostly bug fixes and small improvements to performance and stability, the latest developer release for iOS 27 did introduce some more substantive changes. 
For example, Siri has several additional voice options, and there's a new splash screen for Siri AI that explains its features when users open it for the first time. There's an adaptive mode slider for AirPods Pro in the Control Center, and the TV app will automatically download upcoming episodes for shows you are watching and remove downloads to manage storage space. You can also adjust how much text is previewed in chat lists, and "Zoom Photos to Fill" allows images to automatically fill your device's display. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Anyone with a compatible device can try Apple's public betas—you'll just need to enroll your Apple Account in Apple's beta program. We've covered the process for both iOS 27 and macOS 27, including which devices can run the update and the potential risks involved with installing a public beta. While public betas are typically safer than developer betas, they're not perfect, and it's always possible that bugs will slip through. At the very least, you'll want to make sure you have a backup of your data, just in case.

title: You Can Now Verify Your Facebook Account With a Video Selfie
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Facebook is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark.
                                            This is a separate feature from Meta Verified, which is a paid subscription for obtaining a blue check mark in Facebook and Instagram.
                                            You'll record a short selfie video, which Facebook will compare to other profile photos, but you should consider whether you want to provide more data to Meta.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're on Facebook, you may soon see a new type of verification badge on user profiles meant to indicate that there is a real, live person behind them. The platform is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark, which will appear on their profile and across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups. (At launch, badges won't appear in Feed posts, but Facebook says that feature will be added in the future.)Note that this is different from Meta Verified, a paid subscription that provides the blue check mark to accounts on Facebook and Instagram. This verification indicates that Meta has confirmed the user's identity based on a review of their government-issued ID and, in some cases, a selfie video. How Facebook Verified worksFacebook Verified is available to users age 18 and older whose accounts are in good standing with the platform's community standards, though the feature is launching in select markets initially before being rolled out globally. Once you have access, you'll need to record a short video selfie, which Facebook will compare to existing profile photos on your account using facial recognition. If your verification is approved, the white check mark will be added to your profile. Verification is not available for Pages or ProMode accounts. 
Consider your privacy firstFacebook says it will store your selfie video for "up to 30 days" after verification, which is a one-time process. It's not entirely clear what happens with that video in the meantime, and it's worth noting that Meta has relied on user data to train its AI. Meta AI (and Meta more broadly) is a terrible offender when it comes to privacy and security, so you should consider whether the tradeoff of a verification mark is worth handing over more of your data and read the privacy policy before you agree. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Google also launched a video selfie verification feature this week, though its purpose is to prove your identity should you get locked out of your account. Unlike Facebook Verified, which is meant to be a trust signal to other users, Google's selfie verification allows access to your entire Google account, bringing with it some additional security considerations.

title: Google Is Rolling Out a Video-Selfie Option If You Get Locked Out of Your Account
body:
David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Google
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google is adding a new video selfie sign-in option for user accounts.
                                            You can use it for identity verification if you're having trouble logging in.
                                            The feature seems to be available for some but not all users right now.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Finding yourself locked out of your Google account for whatever reason is a stressful situation to be in—what with all your emails, documents, photos, and other data suddenly out of bounds—but there's now a new way to prove your identity and regain access: a simple selfie video.It's always wise to have multiple sign-in methods set up, beyond the basic password and email address, as each additional one gives you a better chance of getting your account back if something goes wrong. The recovery contacts feature is a good example, where Google uses verified, trusted contacts of yours to prove your identity.Now you can also use a selfie video. By following this link you can see if the feature is live for your account, and record your selfie via a webcam or phone camera. If you're having trouble logging in, you'll be able to record a new selfie, which will be compared against the original saved in your account.
At the moment, the selfie video option for my account isn't available, so I couldn't test it out. It seems this will be rolled out gradually to users, though Google hasn't said anything specific about availability or a schedule—just that users can now check if their account is eligible."Your selfie video is yours and you're in control," says Google in its announcement blog post. "It is recorded and securely stored with your consent, and you can delete it at any time in your Google Account. It's used only for helping you sign in, unless you opt to share it for additional purposes. Your selfie video is encrypted at rest, meaning it's securely stored even when it's not being used."Those "additional purposes"  mean that Google will use your "video and related data to help ongoing efforts to develop and improve facial recognition, age estimation, and other verification methods that may use your physical features or movement" (the specter of age verification looms large again).
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
There's also the rather obvious issue of deepfakes. Google says there are "multiple layers of security" to guard against fake photos and videos, including getting you to go through several simple movements when recording the selfie—movements that are hard to predict and mimic with a deepfake.All of the usual Google account checks will be in force too, so (for example) you might find additional security questions pop up if you're suddenly trying to log in from the other side of the world from where your usual login attempts are.Given the accuracy of technologies like Face ID these days, video selfie sign-in should prove to be a useful backup method of accessing your account. There's nothing extra for you to remember—you just have to bring your face—and it appears at the moment to be difficult to get around.

title: These Four New Android Features Are Coming, but Samsung Galaxy Devices Will Get Them First
body:
David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 22, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Google
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Samsung's new phones come with extra Gemini features.
                                            The Galaxy Watch 9 is getting a Gemini upgrade, too.
                                            Google has also announced "streamlined switching" from iPhones.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Amid another busy Galaxy Unpacked event and the reveal of several new Samsung foldables and smartwatches, there's also news from Google in partnership with Samsung: Several new Android features are going to show up first on the Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Z Flip 8, before appearing on Pixels and other phones.This has become something of a tradition with Samsung's mid-year product launches, as a smattering of new features—including gaming support for Circle to Search—appeared first on the Galaxy Z Fold 7 and Galaxy Z Flip 7 last year.For 2026, the emphasis is on Gemini. First, the Gemini Intelligence feature that completes tasks for you, launched in beta in May, is being expanded to support more than 40 apps and is available out of the box on the new Galaxy foldables. Plus, you can launch your agentic assistant with a screengrab now as well as a prompt (so maybe a picture of an item of clothing you want the AI to look for online).
Google hasn't specified which 40 apps are now included, but the idea is the same as before: Gemini can carry out more admin for you, like booking cabs or reserving tables, in your apps. You'll still get an overview of what the AI is up to on your screen, as well as final approval on any important actions, and you can stop the process at any time.
    
            
            Gemini Notebook is preinstalled on the new Samsung phones.
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
Next up is the newly rebranded Gemini Notebook (the AI research tool previously known as NotebookLM). There are no new features here, but the app is going to be preinstalled on the foldables that Samsung just unveiled, and on the Z Fold 8 devices, you can take advantage of the wider screen to drag and drop elements (such as images and web links) into your notebooks from other apps.Additionally, if you buy a Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, or Galaxy Z Flip 8, you get six months of Google AI Pro for free (usually $19.99 a month). Compared to the free tier, Google AI Pro gets you video generation, the Antigravity coding tool, YouTube Premium Lite, 5TB of storage to play with, and significantly higher usage limits across all of Google's AI tools (including Gemini and Gemini Notebook).
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The third Gemini perk for those investing in a new Samsung device applies to the Galaxy Watch 9. On the new smartwatch, Gemini will start listening for instructions as soon as you raise your wrist to talk—no wake word required. It's a small tweak, but means you'll get faster access to the AI.Lastly, Google has also announced "streamlined switching" from iPhones, built into Android 17 and available on the new Samsung phones. You'll no longer need a cable, as it now works wirelessly, and extra data types are now supported as well—including your Google Account details and wifi credentials, on top of photos, videos, contacts, messages, and calendars.This improved switching method has already started rolling out on Pixel devices, Google says, and will, reportedly, soon be showing up on other Android devices as well.

title: It's Not Just You: YouTube's Picture-in-Picture Isn't Working
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 20, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: 5./15 WEST via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            As of Monday morning, YouTube's picture-in-picture (PiP) mode is broken for some users.
                                            YouTube has confirmed the issue, and says it is working on a fix.
                                            The issue appears to affect both iOS and Android, but is reportedly much more common on iPhone.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Picture-in-picture (PiP) is great for us multitaskers. While some prefer to pay full attention to their content, others prefer to keep videos running while attending to other tasks. I frequently have a video playing in PiP on both my iPhone and Mac, while I scan headlines, chat with friends, or take care of any to-do that only requires half my focus. While there are ways to manually trigger PiP, it's best on mobile, as most video player apps have adopted a natural method: When you play a video, you can simply leave the app, and the video continues playing in a PiP window. It's now muscle memory for me on iOS: I head to YouTube, choose a video, and swipe out of the app, knowing my video will keep running as I move to other apps on my iPhone.       YouTube PiP is broken (especially on iOS)Of course, like most things, PiP is only good when it works. You might have recently tried the exact shortcut I just described, only to find that nothing actually happens. You close out of YouTube, but your video doesn't follow in a PiP window. (Though it may still continue to play in the background.) And while some of you might be Android users, I'd be willing to bet most are on iPhones. What gives? 
As reported by 9to5Google, YouTube is currently experiencing issues with PiP. This isn't something only a handful of users are dealing with. The problem is apparently so widespread, YouTube has confirmed the issue directly. In a statement on YouTube Help, a Google employee shared the following:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
"We're aware that some of you are experiencing issues with the Picture-in-Picture (PiP) feature failing to trigger when exiting the YouTube app. While the vast majority of these reports are coming from iOS users, we are also seeing a significantly lower volume of reports from Android users...Our teams are actively investigating the issue, and we'll update this thread as soon as we have more information." At the time of writing, over 11,600 users hit the "I have the same question" button on this YouTube Help post. Is there any way to fix PiP in the YouTube app?Unfortunately, it doesn't seem like there is any workaround. For what it's worth, PiP was intermittent for me this morning in the YouTube app on iOS. I had no problem swiping out of a video into PiP mode during an ad, but once the video started playing, PiP didn't work. Not only that, but playback stopped as well. I went back to YouTube, played the video again, and when I left the app this time, PiP kicked in. This continued on and off, not working one time, but working the next.

body:
Daniel Oropeza
                            
        
            Daniel Oropeza
                
                                            Shopping Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceDaniel is Lifehacker's Shopping Editor covering tech deals and reviewing TVs, headphones, speakers, and projectors. He earned his master’s in journalism from Columbia University and has reported for the Miami Herald. He lives in Atlanta.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 27, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
            Deal pricing and availability subject to change after time of publication.
    
            Credit: Woot/Lifehacker 
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you've been patiently waiting for the right moment to pull the trigger on the best Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal like I have, this is the part where your patience gets rewarded. Woot is selling a refurbished Nintendo Switch 2 Mario Kart World Bundle for $419. That's $80 less than the retail price for a new bundle and arguably better than the deal they had in June, as long as you don't mind a refurbished unit.
This bundle deal is a great opportunity when you consider the console by itself (without the bundle) will increase to $499.99 come Sept. 1. Since we're about a month away from that date, this could very well be the last great opportunity to buy the console for its lowest price.The new console is an upgrade in every way, as you can read in our full review of the Nintendo Switch 2. The ergonomics and design have improved, making it much better to hold and look at. The battery life has also improved, now with about 180 minutes of handheld playtime before the juice runs out.A big plus is that the Switch 2 is backwards-compatible: You can play your old Switch games on it. Some Switch games have the ability to upgrade to the Switch 2 Edition by buying that game's upgrade pack. This is especially worth it for games like The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, which will look better on the Switch 2.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
There aren't many Switch 2 games out at the moment, but there are some classic Nintendo games to keep you busy until the library expands, like Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, and Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment. If you already own a Switch 2, check out our Top 10 Hacks to get the most out of your device.

            Credit: Lifehacker
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            NotebookLM is being rebranded as Gemini Notebook.
                                            It will still work closely with the main Gemini AI app.
                                            More features are now rolling out to Google AI Pro accounts.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        NotebookLM may not be the most well-known of Google's numerous AI products, but having been introduced as Project Tailwind in May 2023, it's actually been around almost as long as the Google Gemini chatbot (originally called Bard, as you might remember).Now, perhaps in a bid to make its suite of AI tools a little less confusing, Google is renaming NotebookLM as Gemini Notebook. If you love the app in its current form, though, don't panic—not much else is changing."It remains a standalone product ... but it will now do more across the Google ecosystem, including inside the Gemini app and Google Search," explains Google. That "do more" will start with your notebooks appearing in AI Mode in Google Search for reference, which is rolling out soon.
Google's announcement post also mentions that users on the Pro plans ($19.99 a month) will soon be getting the upgrades rolled out last month, which were previously exclusive to Ultra plan users ($99.99 or $199.99 a month).These upgrades include a dedicated cloud computer for each notebook you create, enabling deeper analysis of sources and the ability to write and execute code natively (via Google Antigravity). It also means more capabilities in terms of what the app can do within each of your notebooks, including creating PDFs, charts, and slideshows, and editing them through prompts.
    
            
            The new branding for Gemini Notebook.
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
Where Gemini ends and Gemini Notebook beginsYou could be forgiven for getting confused about the difference between the standard Gemini AI chatbot app you find on the web and mobile, and the newly renamed Gemini Notebook—especially if you've not used the latter much.They run on the same set of Gemini AI models, and can do a lot of the same tasks in terms of looking up information from the web and summarizing documents. When you've created notebooks inside Gemini Notebook, you can then also access them in the main Gemini app, confusing things even further.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What makes Gemini Notebook different is that it's very much a research tool. You load up a bunch of sources, from YouTube videos to PDFs, and then get Gemini Notebook to query and summarize those sources, with citations.As we've written about before, you can turn your notes into audio podcasts and video overviews, as well as mind maps, flashcards, infographics and slideshows. Unlike the main Gemini app, though, it can't create images or videos out of a single prompt, without one or more sources to work from.As an addendum: If you're already a seasoned NotebookLM/Gemini Notebook user, you may have missed the latest feature upgrade, rolled out to all users a couple of weeks ago. It's called Short Video Overview, and adds a shorter, vertical video format for your summary options: Click Video Overview then Short to use it.

title: MacOS 27 Comes With a Hidden Siri AI Menu
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 20, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple's latest macOS 27 beta comes with a hidden Siri AI menu.
                                            Once engaged, you'll see a Siri AI shortcut whenever you highlight text.
                                            You can enable the feature with a Terminal command, but it may be unstable or buggy at this time.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Siri AI is the biggest feature of Apple's upcoming suite of updates. Whether you're running iOS 27, macOS 27, or even watchOS 27, the thing that you'll likely notice first (assuming you're running a compatible device) is that Siri is much smarter now, and even more capable than it was in previous versions. If the beta previews have been any indication, this really is the biggest upgrade Apple has ever given Siri.  But it seems that the company isn't limiting itself to the upgrades it already announced. As it continues beta testing these new updates, and with them, Siri AI itself, Apple seems to be tinkering with its new AI-powered assistant, quietly planting new features that beta testers need to discover for themselves. One such feature? A new Siri AI menu that appears whenever you highlight text in macOS 27. As reported by MacRumors, this new menu appears whenever you select text in macOS 27. When you do, you'll see a floating menu in the top left of your highlighted text. If you move your cursor over it, the menu expands to reveal options, such as "Proofread," "Rewrite," "How does this sound?" and "Edit with Siri." You can also ask Siri AI to pull out key points from the text, or summarize it completely. Depending on the text, you might see other options, too: If you highlight a text from a friend, Siri AI might show you contact info; if the text contains a date, Siri AI might prompt you to create a Calendar entry. It plays into Siri AI's contextual awareness, which is part of Apple's mission to make its assistant more useful in specific scenarios. 
The thing is, this menu is disabled by default, as least as of macOS 27 developer beta 3 and public beta 1. Apple did not include it in the release notes, either; instead, a Redditor stumbled upon it, and shared instructions for turning it on on r/MacOSBeta.   Keep in mind, this feature, as with macOS 27 as a whole, is in beta testing. MacRumors says that the feature does not always work, so you may run into odd bugs or glitches after turning it on. Still, if you're already running the beta and are curious, this is an interesting feature to explore. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
To try it out, you'll need to open your Mac's Terminal app. Then, paste and run the following command: sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain && sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/WritingTools LightweightUI_macOS -dict Enabled -bool trueYou'll need to restart your Mac for the feature to take effect. But once you do, you should see the menu whenever you highlight text—albeit with some possible hiccups. If the feature is too unstable at this point, or you simply don't like it, you can undo it by pasting the following command into Terminal: sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/WritingTools LightweightUI_macOS -dict Enabled -bool false

title: That LastPass or Bitwarden Security Email May Be a Scam
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 17, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Zooey Liao/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        You trust your password manager to keep your credentials, documents, and identity data secure—and you probably also trust notices that come from your password manager with steps to maintain that security. Scammers are counting on this: A new phishing campaign is targeting LastPass and Bitwarden users with fake security alerts designed to compromise their data and devices. Earlier this week, LastPass alerted users to an impersonation scam in which threat actors are sending phishing emails that look like official security notices. The messages come from hello[at]lastpassnewsletter[.]com with the subject line "Action Required: Review Updated LastPass Security Policies." In the email body, attackers outlined supposed changes to LastPass security monitoring and reporting protocols and noted that users "have 14 business days to review and accept the updated terms" via DocuSign. The link redirected to https[:]//lastpasscompliance[.]com/, which looked like a legitimate DocuSign page complete with a chatbot window, and prompted users to "download" DocuSign in order to review and sign the document. It's unclear whether the goal was to spread malware or harvest user credentials, as the malicious website has since been taken down. However, Bitwarden users have been targeted with a nearly identical campaign, according to BleepingComputer. 
How to spot the password manager scamOn the surface, the phishing emails targeting LastPass and Bitwarden users are pretty convincing. They have some technical jargon, so users may skim over the specifics and trust that the information is legitimate. There's a call to action, but the email states that users have 14 days to accept the terms or their account "may be temporarily restricted"—so the urgency is slightly lower than with some other scams. The email even reassures users that their vaults and accounts are "completely secure" and states that the required steps are "strictly" administrative in nature.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
That said, both the sender and the URL should raise suspicion. Neither lastpassnewsletter[.]com nor lastpasscompliance[.]com are official LastPass domains, nor is bitwardencompliance[.]com a real Bitwarden site. Never enter your master password or other credentials unless you navigate directly to your password manager's website or vault—links from emails, texts, or social media messages are at risk of being phishing attempts. If you've supplied your credentials to a suspicious site, update them immediately from a trusted device. You also shouldn't need to download software or use DocuSign for your password manager, and any actions on your account should occur when you are logged in to the legitimate site or vault.

        During its July Unpacked event, Samsung officially unveiled its next-generation of foldable Galaxy devices. There's the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which, despite the name, is really the successor to the Galaxy Z Fold 7. The Galaxy Z Fold 8, instead, is actually a new device, introducing a lighter design (and a slightly smaller price tag) than the Z Fold 8 Ultra. Finally, there's the Z Flip 8, which actually doesn't change much from the Z Flip 7.  If you're in the market for a new foldable smartphone, these new devices might be on your radar. Even the Z Flip 8's minor adjustments might prove a worthwhile upgrade if your Flip device is more than a few years old. While you can't buy one today, you can preorder any of them right now. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is Samsung's premium foldable for 2026. Out of Samsung's newest products, it has the biggest and best cameras (200MP Wide, 50MP Ultra Wide, and 10MP Tele), the largest displays (6.5-inch outer display, 8-inch inner display), the biggest battery (5,000 mAh), and, unfortunately, comes with the biggest price tag. If you're interested, you can preorder from the following links:  
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra (256 GB): $2,099.99 at SamsungSamsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra (512 GB): $2,299.99 at SamsungSamsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra (1TB): $2,699.99 at SamsungHow to preorder the Galaxy Z Fold 8 A lot of people are going to think the Z Fold 8 is the upgraded version of the Z Fold 7, but it's not. This is a lighter take on Samsung's foldable, which might appeal to users who want a phablet that takes up a little less space in their pocket. It comes with a 5.5-inch outer display, a 7.6-inch inner display, three rear cameras (50MP Wide, 50MP Ultra Wide, and 2x Optical Zoom), and the same Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip as the rest of the "Z 8" line. With that lighter framework comes a slightly smaller MSRP (emphasis on slightly), as the Z Fold 8 starts at $1,899.99. Here are the preorder links from Samsung:

Still, it's the company's flagship Z Flip, so if you're looking to upgrade, or thinking about picking up a flip phone for the first time, it's one to consider. title: iOS 26.6 Comes With Two New Features, and One Is Key for iOS 27
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 27, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Thomas Trutschel / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple's next update isn't iOS 27: it's iOS 26.6, which the company rolled out to compatible iPhones on Monday.
                                            The update comes with two features you need to know about, one of which makes it possible to use Siri AI immediately after installing iOS 27.
                                            The other sends you an alert after you've blocked too many contacts on your iPhone, though that exact limit appears unclear.
                                            Finally, iOS 26.6 comes with a series of security updates.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        When you think about a big iPhone update on the horizon, iOS 27 likely comes to mind. And yet, Apple just released a totally different update: iOS 26.6. Typically, iOS updates this close to the launch of the next major version are focused on security fixes and squashing bugs, saving any major changes for the next big numbered update. And while iOS 26.6 comes with these under-the-hood adjustments, it also comes with two new features you should be aware of—including one that actually lays the groundwork for iOS 27.Preparing your iPhone for Siri AIiOS 26.6's first feature won't reveal itself when you install the update on your iPhone. In fact, most of us may think iOS 26.6 has no new features at all. But the update's most important new change is key for compatible iPhones upgrading to iOS 27. As it turns out, iOS 26.6 "optimizes the Spotlight index" on your iPhone to prepare it for iOS 27. In other words, the update gets your iPhone ready for Siri AI. Apple's AI-powered assistant relies on the new search architecture in iOS 27 to run properly. As such, if you install iOS 27 without updating to iOS 26.6 first, it may take days before Siri AI can perform as expected. By preparing your iPhone with iOS 26.6 now, you'll avoid the growing pains.
Of course, that won't benefit everyone eventually upgrading to iOS 27. While the update runs on iPhone 12 and newer devices, only the iPhone 15 Pro and newer can try Siri AI. Still, if that's you, iOS 27's new Siri will run much more smoothly coming from iOS 26.6 than from iOS 26.5.2.     iOS 26.6's other new feature is a new alert, letting you know that you've reached iOS' limit of the number of contacts you can block. It's not clear exactly how many contacts that is, but new code in the update confirms the alert is present. The alert reads: "Blocked Contacts Limit Reached: You’ve reached the maximum number of blocked contacts. To block additional callers, remove a blocked contact in Settings."
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The thing is, there's no documentation of what that limit actually is. In fact, anecdotal evidence suggests that the limit is user-dependent. MacRumors reports that some users receive the alert after blocking 20,000 contacts, while others only get 8,000. I've seen comments suggesting the limit is lower still, with some claiming to hit it in the 5,000s. Nonetheless, that's a lot of blocked contacts, and will likely only apply to users who receive an overwhelming number of calls and messages from unwanted sources. iOS 26.6's security updates and bug patchesLike most of Apple's updates, iOS 26.6 comes with a series of security patches to fix vulnerabilities discovered since the last update—a large number of patches, at that. iOS 26.6 includes nearly 80 of them, likely reflecting Apple's use of AI models to help identify flaws and vulnerabilities. I expect future updates to ship with an increasing number of patches as well. It's not just Apple, either: Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update had a record 570 patches. Luckily, none of the flaws patched in iOS 26.6 were zero-days, so none were actively exploited or publicly disclosed before this update.

title: These Gboard Alternatives Are Open-Source and Privacy-First
body:
Khamosh Pathak
                            
        
            Khamosh Pathak
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceKhamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 16, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Igor Suka/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Gboard is the default keyboard for Pixel smartphones and many devices that use stock Android, but it’s not the only option out there. Recently, Gboard has been swept up in a privacy controversy highlighting how your data is used by Google for its own training and collection. The data that Google collects can be intercepted and tied to individual users. Luckily, you can disable some of those data-sharing settings. But what if, down the line, Gboard changes its policy or privacy settings? Or we learn about additional ways Google sneakily collects your data from your keyboard? If that concerns you, consider using an open-source keyboard that runs completely on device, no data servers required. Unlike closed software, security experts can audit open-source programs, so vulnerabilities are found and patched quite quickly. As it happens, there are two solid open-source alternatives to Gboard. One is so like Gboard, you won’t even miss it. The second is as private as a keyboard gets.FUTO Keyboard is a direct Gboard replacement
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Khamosh Pathak
                    
    
FUTO Keyboard is designed to be a direct Gboard replacement. It looks like Gboard, and it works like Gboard. But underneath, it’s completely open-source, free, and private. By default, none of your keystrokes leave your device.
FUTO includes on-device AI models for text prediction and voice typing. The text prediction model works completely offline and doesn't use any online servers. In my testing, it kept up with my typing, and the suggestions were more or less what you'd expect. For voice typing, the app uses a lightweight Whisper-based model, also running on-device, with no servers involved. In my testing, I found the default model to be a bit underwhelming when compared to Gboard. Downloading the highest-tier model resolved this issue, though, and I saw voice typing results similar to Gboard. (The English-244 voice model is a 280MB download.)
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Khamosh Pathak
                    
    
FUTO gets a lot more fun when you start customizing the settings and the layout. You can resize the keyboard to make it larger, add a permanent numbers row to the top, an arrow bar, and change the theme to your liking. There are also fine-tuning settings for users who like adjusting every bit of how their keyboard works. For example, there is a section on Long-Press Keys that lets you customize how the backspace long-press gesture works.In my testing, I found that the FUTO keyboard offers a smoother, more reliable typing experience compared to Gboard. A small example is the spacebar gesture. In Gboard, you can move the cursor by swiping on the spacebar, but it’s a bit confusing for me. You hold it for a split second, and then swipe. In FUTO, swiping on the spacebar instantly moves the cursor, every single time. The downside to being completely private is, of course, that you lose out on cross-device support. Your personal dictionary, or clipboard, can’t sync between all your devices. While Gboard is a more complete package, FUTO's privacy features do make up for that loss.HeliBoard is the Gboard alternative for security purists
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Khamosh Pathak
                    
    
HeliBoard has a rich open-source pedigree. It’s based on the old OpenBoard project, which itself was based on the pure Android AOSP keyboard, the original stock Android keyboard.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The times have changed, though, and HeliBoard has kept up, without sacrificing its open-source roots. The app promises a zero-exposure experience, asking for no network permissions whatsoever. As this is a purist’s keyboard, there are no AI features to speak of: no LLM transformer for text prediction, no AI voice typing model.That said, all the basic features you’d expect from an Android keyboard are all here. You can add an optional number row to the top, and there’s support for gesture typing, along with an on-device clipboard (which can be disabled). You can customize the appearance as well. You can resize the keyboard, bring back the old Holo keyboard style, change icons, and change the color of the keyboard. (You can even use an image as the background.)The only caveat to using HeliBoard is that it’s not available in the Google Play Store. Instead, you’ll have to download it from the F-Droid third-party app store that specializes in securely hosting free and open-source apps. But that’s easy to do, and once installed, you can explore other useful open-source apps like NewPipe, my preferred way of watching YouTube ad-free on Android.

title: Don’t Watch the Clock When You Can’t Sleep (and Focus on This Instead)
body:
Beth Skwarecki
                            
        
            Beth Skwarecki

        When you can’t sleep, the clock can seem to be taunting you. “At least I’m getting seven hours,” you might think as you lie down, but if you’re still awake an hour later, then you’re only getting six hours, and six isn’t a lot. And if you’re still not tired, then it’s going to be less than six, and eventually you’re just lying in bed thinking about how screwed you’re going to be in the morning.If this sounds familiar, it’s not just you. Sleep scientists have long recognized the idea of “losing sleep over losing sleep,” and it’s a well-known factor that can contribute to insomnia. It’s not necessarily the cause of your sleep problems, but it can make them worse. For example, say you have some minor issue that makes it hard to sleep. You get into a cycle of stressing out over the clock at night, getting poor sleep, and then being tired the next day. Then you begin to dread bedtime, because you know it’s going to happen all over again. Before you know it, you may be taking medications to help you sleep, which have their own health risks (nightly Benadryl is not good for you). A 2023 study found that “time-monitoring behavior,” as they called clock-watching, may be driving people to take medications they wouldn’t otherwise need. So what can you do instead? Here's what sleep experts recommend.Hide the clockOne of the authors of that study says that it can help to promise yourself you won’t look at the time. Turn the clock around, cover the display, or if you use your phone to check the time, put it out of reach. If the alarm hasn’t gone off yet, it’s still nighttime, and that’s all you really need to know. Without the clock, you might worry that you don’t know if you’re getting enough sleep or not. But even with the clock, you aren’t necessarily counting the hours accurately. Those hours you think you’re fully awake, you’re often drifting in and out of sleep, and getting more of it than you think you are. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you sleep with a watch or fitness tracker that tracks your sleep, only pay attention to the data if it's helping you. If you check your data in the morning and think "hm, I got more sleep than I realized," that's reassuring. But if checking the data ends up adding to your anxiety, try to get out of the habit of checking the app. Trackers aren't always 100% accurate anyway, and you may feel more tired if you think you slept poorly, even if your sleep was actually OK. Also consider these tips on how to use sleep tracking data more healthily. 
Focus on relaxingHere's a reassuring thought for those late nights: relaxation, even if you're awake, is almost as good as sleep. Close your eyes and calm your mind, and most importantly, tell yourself that this is exactly what your body needs right now. Relaxing this way may give you some of the benefits of meditation, and there’s even a hypothesis that meditation gives you some of the benefits of sleep. Whether it’s true or not, it’s a comforting thought when you’re lying awake in the middle of the night. And if you need one more reason to stop worrying, remember that relaxation is one of the best ways to get to sleep—so whether you fall asleep or not, you’re helping your body and brain by finding a restful way to spend the remaining hours of the night.
